title: Echoes of an Older Tongue
text:
Literary authors have long exploited archaic vocabulary to lend their prose an air of gravity or nostalgia. A word such as 'ere' or 'wherefore' carries no precise informational load for most modern readers, yet its very strangeness signals that the text belongs to another epoch. Consequently, the archaic register operates less as a conduit of content than as an atmosphere. Such atmospheric effects are notoriously difficult to render in translation, since equivalent archaisms rarely exist across languages.

Philologists, however, caution that archaism is seldom a simple return to the past. Authors reconstruct older forms selectively, often blending centuries of usage into a composite that never existed in any single period. The result is a stylised idiom whose authenticity is, in a sense, fictional. Readers who recognise this artifice may find the text more rewarding, for it reveals the author's conscious negotiation with tradition.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what do archaic words signal to modern readers?
options: That the text belongs to another epoch
That the author is a scientist
That the content is entirely factual

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what do philologists caution about archaism?
options: It is seldom a simple return to the past
It always reproduces a single historical period
It makes texts impossible to read
It is used only in translated works

questions.text: What can be inferred about the atmosphere created by archaic vocabulary?
options: It can be hard to translate because equivalent archaisms may not exist
It is easy to reproduce in any language
It depends mainly on the factual accuracy of the content
It is created only by modern slang

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about readers who recognise the artifice in a stylised text?
options: They may appreciate how the author negotiates tradition
They will find the text less interesting
They will reject all literary archaism
They will assume the text is historically exact

vocabulary.definition: old words or expressions no longer in ordinary use
scholars who study language in historical texts
a clever but artificial device or pretence

paragraph_translations: Autores literários há muito exploram o vocabulário arcaico para dar à sua prosa um ar de seriedade ou nostalgia. Uma palavra como 'ere' ou 'wherefore' não carrega nenhuma carga informativa precisa para a maioria dos leitores modernos, mas sua estranheza revela que o texto pertence a outra época. Consequentemente, o registro arcaico funciona menos como um canal de conteúdo do que como uma atmosfera. Esses efeitos atmosféricos são notoriamente difíceis de traduzir, pois arcaísmos equivalentes raramente existem em outras línguas.

Os filólogos, porém, alertam que o arcaísmo raramente é um simples retorno ao passado. Os autores reconstroem formas antigas de maneira seletiva, muitas vezes misturando séculos de uso em um composto que nunca existiu em nenhum período isolado. O resultado é um idioma estilizado cuja autenticidade é, em certo sentido, ficcional. Leitores que reconhecem esse artifício podem achar o texto mais gratificante, pois ele revela a negociação consciente do autor com a tradição.
